en: Departing from what is normal or accepted
hook: AB-ERR-ANT: ERRing AWAY from the norm.
story: The usually polite student's aberrant behavior, shouting at teachers and skipping classes, worried his parents; something was clearly wrong. Aberrant means deviating from the normal. Synonyms: anomalous, deviant. An aberration is an unusual event.

en: To tolerate; to accept or act in accordance with a rule
hook: ABIDE: can't ABIDE it = can't stand it. ABIDE BY = obey.
story: Mitu's mother cannot abide lies; she forgives mistakes but never dishonesty. All drivers must abide by traffic laws. To abide means to tolerate, usually in the negative, or to abide by means to obey.

en: A bold show of courage meant to impress, often hiding fear
hook: BRAVADO: BRAVE-looking, but just a show.
story: Before the big exam, Rafi announced with bravado, 'Easy! I'll finish in half the time.' But his hands were shaking. Bravado is a show of boldness intended to impress, often covering fear. Synonyms: swagger, bluster.

en: To permit; also, to admit or concede that something is true
hook: GRE trick: ALLOW can mean ADMIT — 'he allowed that he was wrong.'
story: The teacher allowed the students to use calculators. Later, she allowed that the test had been too difficult, admitting her mistake. Allow usually means to permit, but in formal writing it can mean to concede or acknowledge.

en: To surrender or give in
hook: CAPITULATE: surrender your CAPITAL city.
story: After weeks of protests, the management capitulated, agreeing to every one of the workers' demands. In 1971, the Pakistani army capitulated in Dhaka. To capitulate is to stop resisting and give in. Synonyms: surrender, yield.

en: To think deeply about something
hook: COGITATE: 'Cogito, ergo sum' — I think, therefore I am.
story: Before deciding which university to choose, Tanvir cogitated for weeks, making lists, comparing costs, and imagining his future in each city. To cogitate is to think deeply and carefully. Synonyms: ponder, ruminate, contemplate.

en: A person's behavior and manners; the way one carries oneself
hook: DEPORTMENT: how you COMPORT yourself.
story: The finishing school taught deportment: how to walk gracefully, sit straight, eat politely, and speak calmly. Even years later, Nadia's posture was perfect. Deportment means manners and bearing. Synonyms: demeanor, conduct.

en: To speak or perform without preparation; to improvise
hook: EX-TEMPOR-IZE: OUT of the moment (tempus = time).
story: When the chief guest didn't show up, the host had to extemporize a fifteen-minute speech on the spot. Nobody could tell it wasn't planned. To extemporize is to improvise. Extempore speeches are given without preparation.

en: Inclined to cause disagreement and division into factions
hook: FACTIOUS: creating FACTIONS.
story: The club's factious members constantly formed groups against each other, and every meeting ended in shouting. Nothing ever got done. Factious means causing division. Don't confuse it with fractious (irritable) or facetious (joking).

en: Of land: left unplanted to restore fertility; inactive
hook: FALLOW: the field just lies there, FALLEN asleep.
story: Farmers sometimes leave a field fallow for a season so the soil can recover. After graduating, Sara had a fallow year: no job, no study, just rest and reading. Fallow means unused or inactive, often temporarily.

en: A deceptive movement meant to distract an opponent
hook: FEINT: a FAKE move. Sounds like FAINT but means FAKE.
story: The footballer made a feint to the left, the defender jumped that way, and he slipped right and scored. A feint is a deceptive move. Boxers feint punches to trick their opponents. Synonym: ruse.

en: Shockingly obvious and offensive
hook: FLAGRANT: as obvious as a FLAG waving in your face.
story: Building a ten-story tower on a canal, in front of the city office, was a flagrant violation of the law. Nobody even tried to hide it. Flagrant means glaringly obvious and shocking. Synonyms: blatant, egregious.

en: Unnecessary and unjustified; given free of charge
hook: GRATUITOUS: like a GRATUITY (tip), extra and not required.
story: The film's gratuitous violence, endless scenes of blood with no purpose to the story, upset many viewers. Gratuitous means unnecessary and uncalled for. Its older meaning is free of charge, like a gratuity.

en: To behave in an excessively humble way to win favor or forgiveness
hook: GROVEL: crawling in the GRAVEL begging.
story: After being caught lying, the employee groveled before his boss: 'Please, sir, forgive me, I'll never do it again, I'll work for free!' To grovel is to beg in a humiliating way. Synonyms: fawn, kowtow.

en: Not in keeping with good taste and propriety
hook: IN-DECOROUS: NOT showing DECORUM.
story: Laughing loudly and taking selfies during the funeral prayer was indecorous; the elders were deeply offended. Indecorous means improper and in poor taste. Synonyms: unseemly, unbecoming.

en: A secret plot or scheme; to arouse curiosity
hook: INTRIGUE: the palace's secret plots that INTRIGUE you.
story: The royal court was full of intrigue: ministers secretly plotting against each other, poison in cups, and whispers in corridors. The mysterious letter intrigued Sara so much she couldn't sleep. Intrigue means a secret plot, or to fascinate.

en: Very small, far below real value; existing in name only
hook: NOMINAL: in NAME only (nomen).
story: The library charges a nominal fee of ten taka a year, just to keep records. The king was only the nominal ruler; real power belonged to the general. Nominal means tiny, or existing in name only.

en: Stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or action
hook: OB-DURATE: DURABLE stubbornness, hardened.
story: Despite the tears of the whole family, the old man remained obdurate: he would not sell the ancestral land, no matter what. Obdurate means stubbornly unyielding. Synonyms: obstinate, intransigent, adamant.

en: Noisy and difficult to control
hook: OBSTREPEROUS: makes an OBSTACLE with noise.
story: The obstreperous fans in the back row shouted, threw bottles, and refused to sit down until security removed them. Obstreperous means noisy and unruly. Synonyms: boisterous, rowdy, unruly.

en: Extremely unpleasant; hateful
hook: ODIOUS: full of ODOR and hatred.
story: Cheating the poor out of their land is an odious crime. Even the lawyers who defended the landlord felt disgusted. Odious means hateful and repulsive. Synonyms: repugnant, abhorrent, detestable.

en: Brave and determined in difficult circumstances
hook: PLUCKY: has PLUCK (courage).
story: The plucky little team from a small village beat the city champions, with players who practiced barefoot on muddy fields. Plucky means courageous and spirited, especially when facing bigger opponents. Synonyms: mettlesome, spunky.

en: Showing unusually early development, especially mental
hook: PRE-COCIOUS: PRE-COOKED early, ripe too soon.
story: At five, the precocious girl read novels, did multiplication in her head, and argued with adults about politics. Precocious means developing early, beyond one's age. A precocious child seems older than their years.

en: Money paid for work or a service
hook: RE-MUNER-ATION: MONEY (munus) given back for work.
story: The job offered attractive remuneration: a good salary, a yearly bonus, and health insurance. Arif accepted immediately. Remuneration means payment for work. Synonyms: compensation, salary, wages.

en: Messy and careless in appearance or work
hook: SLOVENLY: SLOPPY and LOVE-less care.
story: The slovenly roommate left clothes on the floor, dishes in the sink, and food wrappers under the bed. His homework was equally slovenly. Slovenly means messy and careless. Synonyms: sloppy, untidy.

en: A speech in which a character speaks their thoughts aloud alone
hook: SOLI-LOQUY: SOLO speech (loqui = speak).
story: In Hamlet's famous soliloquy, 'To be or not to be,' he speaks his deepest thoughts aloud, alone on stage. A soliloquy is a speech made to oneself. Tanvir's late-night soliloquies to his mirror before exams amused his roommate.

en: To reject with contempt
hook: SPURN: kick away with your SPUR.
story: The proud scientist spurned the company's offer of millions, refusing to let her research be used for weapons. To spurn is to reject scornfully. Synonyms: rebuff, scorn, repudiate.

en: Calm and showing little emotion; dull
hook: STOLID: SOLID as a stone, no emotion shows.
story: Even when told he'd won the lottery, the stolid farmer just nodded, said 'Good,' and returned to his field. Stolid means calm and unemotional, sometimes dull. Synonyms: impassive, phlegmatic, stoic.

en: Excessive boldness; audacity
hook: TEMERITY: TEMPTING fate with nerve.
story: The junior employee had the temerity to tell the CEO, in front of everyone, that his strategy was foolish. Temerity means reckless boldness. Synonyms: audacity, gall, nerve. Its opposite is timidity.

en: Very weak or slight
hook: TENUOUS: as THIN as a thread.
story: The link between the suspect and the crime was tenuous: just a shoe print that could have belonged to anyone. The judge dismissed the case. Tenuous means weak or flimsy. A tenuous friendship could break at any moment.

en: Vigor and spirit; enthusiasm
hook: VERVE: VIGOR + NERVE.
story: The young dancer performed with such verve, leaping, spinning, and smiling, that the audience couldn't stop clapping. Verve means energy and enthusiasm. Synonyms: vitality, vivacity, panache.
